issues.description: The problem statement and UML specify an addGuestStudents method with a single int parameter (addGuestStudents(int): void). The template, however, provides a method with a different signature: addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, boolean validateInput). This parameter mismatch will confuse students about the required method signature and prevent them from implementing or compiling the expected addGuestStudents(int) method (and will also mismatch automated tests or the solution).
issues.suggested_fix: Change the template method signature to match the specification: declare public void addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents) (no boolean parameter). If input validation is desired, implement it inside that single-parameter method or provide an overloaded private/helper method (e.g. private void addGuestStudents(int, boolean)) so the public API matches the problem statement and the solution.

issues.description: The problem statement (and the reference solution) specify an addGuestStudents(int) method that accepts a single integer parameter. However, the template declares addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents, boolean validateInput) with an extra boolean parameter. This mismatch in method signature creates a mapping barrier: students reading the problem expect to implement a single-argument method, but the provided starter code requires two arguments. It also conflicts with the solution implementation and likely with the automated tests which expect addGuestStudents(int), causing confusion and compilation/test failures.
issues.suggested_fix: Make the template method signature match the problem statement and solution by changing the template to declare public void addGuestStudents(int numberOfNewGuestStudents) (single parameter) and perform any input validation internally. Alternatively, if the boolean flag was intentional, update the problem statement and the reference solution to document and use the two-parameter signature consistently. Prefer aligning the template to the problem/solution to avoid student confusion and test mismatch.
